newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Ukraine deputies pass '97 budget, Kuchma cross.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ukraine deputies pass '97 budget, Kuchma cross.

text.p: Parliament in Ukraine finally approved this year's budget on Friday but President Leonid Kuchma, clearly irritated by the record delay, said he might extend its term to give deputies more time to swallow reforms.
"This is pretty impressive. Here it is, June 27 and they have a budget for 1997," a Western diplomat said sarcastically.

The delay cost Ukraine one reformist deputy prime minister, months of badly-needed cash from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and some of the trust of foreign investors already turned off by widespread government corruption.

Kuchma, speaking two hours after the conservative-dominated chamber passed the draft, said he was thinking about making them work an extra year -- or else they would slack off when they reconvened in September to campaign for elections in March 1998.
"I am ready to consider the question of extending parliament's duties by one year," Kuchma told an audience full of deputies, including Speaker Olexander Moroz.
"Otherwise they will just take a holiday and get involved in pre-election campaigning," he said at the start of a concert marking the first anniversary of the constitution on Saturday.
Some people in the packed audience at Kiev's Opera House whistled and jeered and several deputies said it was a bad idea.

They noted that the constitution says parliament is elected for a four-year term. "You cannot celebrate the first anniversary of the consitution and propose to violate it at the same time," liberal Volodymyr Shcherban said.

The constitution states Kuchma can call early elections if he disbands parliament but does not mention extending its term. "Probably Kuchma is afraid the next parliament will be even more conservative," nationalist deputy Ivan Zayats said.
He was doubtful that a parliament which took six months to pass a budget would have any more luck with radical tax reforms also under consideration since the start of the year.

"If they can't succeed in half a year, they won't succeed in a year and a half," he said, adding it was a bad idea to extend the term of a conservative-dominated chamber with "no wish at all to support reforms".
Socialist speaker Moroz, who had coaxed and pleaded with deputies to pass the budget before the first anniversary of the constitution, looked on sceptically as Kuchma spoke.
Deputies passed the budget by 229 to 71 with 11 abstentions and 27 unregistered votes -- after originally passing the draft in December and returning it to the government for major amendments.
They agreed a deficit of 5.7 percent of gross domestic product, four percent by Western calculations, revenues of 22.4 billion hryvnias and expenditures of 28.12 billion hryvnias.
Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Pynzenyk quit in anger in April over delays in the document, one of 41 conditions Ukraine must meet for a new multi-billion-dollar IMF loan.
IMF representative Patrick Lenain said earlier the Fund might replace the long-term loan with an interim, stand-by deal if Ukraine did not meet its entire wish list by next month.
The budget was to be backed by nine tax reform laws penned by arch-reformer Pynzenyk, but only two have been passed -- on value added tax and on business profit tax.
Pynzenyk's corruption-busting package included scrapping licenses for investors and a system where businesses could avoid bankruptcy by simply declaring they could not pay their taxes.
Parliament is to debate the rest when it reopens in September, but Lenain said the IMF might reconsider the EFF if the list was not complete when the session ends in mid-July.
